content: White tea is a type of tea that is processed using relatively low heat and without rolling. During its production, the leaves undergo an extended period of withering, during which enzymatic reactions occur under carefully controlled conditions of temperature, humidity, and airflow. The goal of this process is to allow the fresh tea leaves to mature with minimal oxidation. White tea typically consists of buds and young leaves, which are known to contain lower levels of caffeine compared to older leaves. This suggests that some white teas may have slightly less caffeine than green teas. White tea is a specialty of Fujian Province in China, and its leaves are derived from various tea cultivars, the most notable being Da Bai (Large White), Xiao Bai (Small White), Narcissus, and Chaicha bushes. Depending on the standards of picking and selection, white teas are classified into different grades. Historically, during times of hardship, impoverished Chinese families would serve guests boiled water when they could not afford tea. They would refer to this water as white tea to maintain the tradition of serving tea to guests, even though it was plain boiled water. This practice is linked to the Chinese term for plain boiled water, white boiled water. Varieties of White Tea Chinese White Teas Bai Hao Yinzhen (Silver Needle): This is the highest grade of white tea. The best Bai Hao Yinzhen should have fleshy, bright-colored buds covered with fine white hairs. The shape of the buds should be uniform, with no stems or leaves. The finest Yinzhen is harvested between March 15 and April 10, during dry weather, using only undamaged and unopened buds. This tea originates from Fujian Province, China. Bai Mu Dan (White Peony): A grade below Bai Hao Yinzhen, this tea includes the bud and two leaves, which should be covered with a fine, silvery-white down. It is also from Fujian Province, China, and is sometimes spelled as Pai Mu Tan. Gong Mei (Tribute Eyebrow): This is the third grade of white tea, made from leaves of the Xiao Bai or small white tea trees. Shou Mei (Noble, Long Life Eyebrow): A fruity and slightly furry white tea, Shou Mei is a mix of tips and upper leaves. It has a stronger flavor compared to other white teas, resembling oolong tea. It is the fourth grade of white tea and is harvested later than Bai Mu Dan, which may result in a darker color. This tea is produced in Fujian Province and Guangxi Province, China. Other White Teas Ceylon White: This is a highly prized tea grown in Sri Lanka. It commands much higher prices than black tea from the same region. Ceylon White tea has a very light liquor with notes of pine and honey, and it produces a golden-coppery infusion. Darjeeling White: This tea has a delicate aroma and brews into a pale golden cup with a mellow taste and a hint of sweetness. It is particularly fluffy and light and originates from Darjeeling, India. Assam White: White tea production in the Assam region is rare. This tea is much lighter in body than traditional black teas from Assam. It yields a refined infusion that is naturally sweet with a distinct malty character. White Pu-erh Tea: This tea is harvested in the spring from plantations located high on remote mountain peaks in Yunnan Province, China. The production process is incredibly labor-intensive, with each step performed by hand. These luxury white teas are rich in fragrance and possess an alluring, sweet, nectar-like quality. Potential Health Benefits White Tea Compared to Green Tea A 2004 study conducted at Pace University demonstrated that white tea possesses greater antiviral and antibacterial properties than green tea. White tea contains higher levels of catechins due to its minimal processing. Catechin concentration is highest in fresh, unbroken, and unfermented tea leaves. Additionally, a study comparing the composition of brewed green and white teas found that white tea contains more gallic acid, theobromine, and caffeine. However, white tea has less fluoride than green tea because it is made exclusively from young leaves. Preparation Guidelines To prepare white tea, use 5 teaspoons of tea per cup and water heated to 80°C (180°F), avoiding boiling water. Steep the tea for 2 to 3 minutes. Some tea experts prefer to brew white tea for much longer, up to 10 minutes for the first infusion, to allow the delicate aromas to fully develop. High-quality white teas reveal more flavor and complexity without bitterness, while lower-grade teas may develop bitter flavors or tannins if brewed for too long. For successive brews (white teas can produce three excellent brews and a fourth that is acceptable), extend the steeping time by several minutes for each infusion. The third brew may require up to 15 minutes to develop properly. Temperature control is crucial; if the water is too hot, the brew will become bitter, and the finer flavors will be overpowered.
